title: Goodbye Toby

jokes.text: Jim pairs Dwight's cell phone to his own headset and begins taking Dwight's calls as 'Dwight Schrute'
jokes.setup: Dwight left his cell phone on his desk unattended
jokes.punchline: 'So, naturally, I paired it to my headset' — Jim's deadpan justification makes the absurd prank feel like the only logical response
jokes.explanation: The joke earns its score because it perfectly captures Jim's character: effortlessly creative, low-key malicious, and delivered with complete nonchalance. The 'naturally' is doing enormous work — it reframes a elaborate prank as the obvious response. The setup is elegant (Dwight's phone, Jim's headset) and the payoff is both the act itself and Jim's justification. High character integration because this is pure Jim.

jokes.text: A caller says 'You sound sexy' and Jim-as-Dwight replies 'Thank you. I've been working out.'
jokes.setup: Jim is impersonating Dwight on his cell phone; a caller flirtatiously says 'oh my goodness, you sound sexy'
jokes.punchline: Jim, staying in character, says 'Thank you. I've been working out' — a perfectly Dwight-like response that is absurdly earnest
jokes.explanation: This is the escalation payoff to the phone prank setup. The line 'Thank you. I've been working out' is pitch-perfect Dwight — vain, literal, and without irony. Jim's commitment to the bit AND the fact that it sounds exactly like something Dwight would say makes this exceptional. Very quotable, high impact in the room.

jokes.text: Dwight demands Jim's earpiece; Jim refuses: 'I can't do that. Unsanitary.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is furious Jim has been taking his calls; demands Jim hand over the earpiece
jokes.punchline: Jim refuses on grounds of sanitation — a fake-reasonable objection that prolongs the bit and infuriates Dwight
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the phone prank cold open. Jim's logic is fake-reasonable, which is classic Jim. Not quite as sharp as the earlier beats but solid.

jokes.text: Jim forwards Dwight's desk phone to his own; answers: 'This is Dwight.' Then aside: 'And I forwarded his desk phone to mine.' A caller says 'Oh hello, mater. Good news, I've married. Tell fater.' Jim: 'Such a nice woman.'
jokes.setup: Dwight thinks he's outsmarted Jim by reprogramming his phone to his office; Jim has anticipated this
jokes.punchline: Jim has already forwarded THAT phone too — and the call turns out to be from Dwight's elderly mother speaking in an archaic/odd dialect, which Jim receives warmly
jokes.explanation: The triple escalation of the cold open — phone → reprogrammed phone → forwarded desk phone — is structurally excellent. Each beat one-ups the last. The payoff of Dwight's mother calling ('mater'... 'fater') is absurdly charming, and Jim's 'Such a nice woman' is a perfect button. This is among the better cold open joke structures the show does: escalating pranks with a humanizing twist.

jokes.text: 'Oh hello, mater. Good news, I've married. Tell fater.' / Jim: 'Such a nice woman.'
jokes.setup: Jim has forwarded Dwight's phone to his own and is answering all calls as Dwight
jokes.punchline: The caller is apparently Dwight's mother, and Jim — completely deadpan — announces to her that 'Dwight' has gotten married, then hangs up and notes warmly 'Such a nice woman.'
jokes.explanation: The capper of the cold open is inspired. Jim has gone from business impersonation to casually altering Dwight's family relationships. 'Tell fater' is a perfect absurdist touch — slightly archaic, weirdly formal — and 'Such a nice woman' delivered as a warm aside is the ideal button. The joke earns a high score because it's original, surprising even within the escalating bit, and deeply in character for Jim's brand of escalating commitment.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'I couldn't sleep last night. I came in extra early. So much energy... I just have a feeling that today is one of those days.'
jokes.setup: This is Toby's last day — a man Michael despises
jokes.punchline: Michael describes his excitement as if it's a joyous occasion, with the language of someone awaiting a wedding or birth — the irony being it's his hated HR rep leaving
jokes.explanation: Well-executed character comedy — Michael's over-the-top joy about Toby leaving is consistent, and the language of 'certain days you'll remember the rest of your life' applied to a coworker's departure is a solid ironic gap. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael greets Kelly instead of Toby: 'Good morning, Kelly. I can't believe this is your last day. How do you feel?'
jokes.setup: Michael is SO focused on Toby leaving that he has confused Kelly for Toby
jokes.punchline: He says 'I can't believe this is your last day' to Kelly, who is baffled — revealing Michael doesn't know his own employees' names/identities
jokes.explanation: Solid Michael character comedy — his obliviousness is played well. The joke is that he's so consumed by Toby's departure he can't even correctly identify people. Functional cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Michael compares Toby's going-away party to a New Orleans funeral parade, then says: 'If the devil were to explode, and evil were gone forever, what sort of party would you have?'
jokes.setup: The party planning committee has a modest plan; Michael wants something grander
jokes.punchline: Michael escalates to a theological metaphor comparing Toby's departure to the death of the devil, framing a party for a mild HR man as a cosmic event
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best Michael-hates-Toby jokes the show ever does. The image is vivid, the hyperbole is perfectly calibrated, and the genuine sincerity with which Michael asks the question makes it funnier. 'If the devil were to explode' is a wildly specific and memorable formulation. High quotability — this line has been repeated by fans. Near the top of the episode.

jokes.text: Angela asks 'Do you mean leaves as in dies?' after Michael's New Orleans funeral parade reference
jokes.setup: Michael says in New Orleans culture, when someone 'leaves' they have a parade
jokes.punchline: Angela deadpans 'Do you mean leaves as in dies?' — cutting through the euphemism with literal bluntness
jokes.explanation: Angela's literalness is good character comedy and a nice beat. Brief but functional.

jokes.text: Michael reveals he's been saving $50/year birthday checks from his grandmother in his shoe — 'And lately she has been sending me, like, nine or ten checks a year'
jokes.setup: Michael wants to fund a lavish going-away party for Toby and pulls out cash from his shoe
jokes.punchline: The detail that grandma is now sending nine or ten checks a year — implying she's mentally declining — is a darkly comic aside delivered with complete obliviousness by Michael
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael obliviousness — he's describing his grandmother's cognitive decline as a financial windfall without recognizing the dark implication. The trailing off ('As Nana starts to...') with no completion is a great structural choice. Genuinely dark and well-executed.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I want a party that makes me feel like I'm flying through the air without this ugly weight holding me down... I want an antigravity machine. I saw it in a movie. You drink a potion and then you just start floating all around.'
jokes.setup: Michael is describing his vision for the party
jokes.punchline: He requests a real antigravity machine based on a movie potion — treating a fantasy prop as an achievable party supply
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist Michael moment — his inability to distinguish movie fantasy from reality is a core character trait. 'You drink a potion and then you just start floating' is charmingly specific. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Phyllis sarcastically: 'So how much antigravity potion do you want?'
jokes.setup: Michael has demanded an antigravity machine with a potion
jokes.punchline: Phyllis plays along with comic deadpan, asking for specifics on the fantasy order
jokes.explanation: Brief but effective. Phyllis playing along with the absurdity rather than calling it out is a nice choice that extends the joke economically.

jokes.text: Pam announces she got into the Pratt School of Design, then admits: 'I didn't read it carefully. I just saw congratulations and skimmed the list. I saw my name, I came in here to tell you and get a snack. Busy morning.'
jokes.setup: Pam bursts in excited about getting into Pratt, acting on the news immediately
jokes.punchline: She hasn't actually finished reading the letter — she's celebrating based on a skim and her primary secondary motive was getting a snack
jokes.explanation: Lovely character moment — 'I came in here to tell you and get a snack. Busy morning' is a perfect Pam line. Warm, relatable, and tells you everything about her impulsive, endearing personality. The anti-climax of the snack motivation is genuinely charming.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'And that is the first time I've ever used the word perfect in here.'
jokes.setup: Pam has just said the timing of going to New York is 'perfect' in her confessional
jokes.punchline: She notes the significance of the word choice, implying that her confessionals have historically been full of doubt and compromise — a meta-acknowledgment of her talking-head history
jokes.explanation: This is a subtle but beautifully crafted line. It rewards long-time viewers who know Pam's confessionals have been full of hedging and sadness. The economy is exceptional — one line carries years of character history. Meta without being showy.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'Oh, strike one. I hate her already.' Michael: 'I hate her too.' Dwight: 'Why do you hate her?' Michael: 'Because she...stinks...with her ways and her...head.'
jokes.setup: Michael has told Stanley that Toby's replacement will be great — Toby's recommendation
jokes.punchline: Stanley reflexively hates her because Toby endorsed her; Michael agrees without reason; when pressed, his 'reason' dissolves into incoherence: 'her ways and her...head'
jokes.explanation: 'Her ways and her...head' is a brilliantly stupid non-reason. Michael's inability to construct even a fake justification for his prejudice is pure character comedy. Stanley's 'strike one' is a great setup line.

jokes.text: Dwight, after Michael chides him for agreeing without thinking: 'Although I will agree that her head is weird.'
jokes.setup: Michael tells Dwight to have original thoughts instead of agreeing with everything he says
jokes.punchline: Dwight attempts an 'original thought' but it's just ratifying Michael's groundless insult about her head
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the exchange. Dwight tries to demonstrate independent thought and fails completely, demonstrating exactly the sycophancy Michael called out. Economy is superb — the irony is packed into one short line.

jokes.text: Michael and Dwight decide to sell Holly an 'elevator pass.' Dwight: 'But our elevator doesn't require a...' Michael: 'Exactly.'
jokes.setup: Michael wants to haze Holly
jokes.punchline: 'But our elevator doesn't require a—' / 'Exactly.' — The joke is that the hazing is selling a pass for something that doesn't exist, and Dwight's partial objection becomes the reveal
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — using Dwight's objection as the punchline delivery is economical and clever. The 'Exactly' button is well-timed. Solid joke construction.

jokes.text: Michael calls to rent 'antigravity machines'; receptionist offers to connect to antidepressants
jokes.setup: Michael is actually calling to source an antigravity machine for the party
jokes.punchline: The receptionist mishears 'antigravity' as 'antidepressant' — a joke about how absurd Michael's request is AND a gentle comedic suggestion
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the antigravity bit with a mild commentary joke. The antidepressant mishearing is an amusing wordplay/observational moment but not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: Holly introduces herself; Michael: 'Oh hey, do you still work here?' to Toby
jokes.setup: Toby brings his replacement to meet Michael
jokes.punchline: Michael greets Toby as if surprised he's still employed — implying he'd already mentally deleted Toby from the office
jokes.explanation: Functional Michael-dismisses-Toby joke. Solid but not exceptional — the hostility-as-forgetfulness gag is well-worn for this character.

jokes.text: Michael to Holly: 'My job is to make the office fun, your job is to make the office lame. And we have an eternal struggle, you and I. And only one of us can be the winner. Spoiler alert... I'm gonna win.'
jokes.setup: Michael is greeting Toby's replacement HR rep for the first time
jokes.punchline: 'Spoiler alert... I'm gonna win' — Michael delivers a faux-dramatic declaration of war to a woman he just met, complete with modern internet slang
jokes.explanation: The 'spoiler alert' usage is well-timed and genuinely funny — Michael treating his HR rivalry as an epic narrative is good character comedy. Works because it's so one-sided and bizarre to deliver to someone you've known for 30 seconds.

jokes.text: Holly to Michael: 'Yeah, I know what you mean. I nearly fell asleep when he gave me a tour of the files.'
jokes.setup: Michael is ranting about how awful Toby is; Holly sympathizes
jokes.punchline: Holly bonds with Michael by revealing Toby bored her too — immediately establishing her as someone who can match Michael's sensibility
jokes.explanation: This joke does double duty — it's funny on its own (Toby is indeed boring) and it's the first signal to the audience that Michael and Holly are compatible. Economical character work.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'I believe that the department is a breeding ground for monsters. What I failed to consider is that not all monsters are bad. Like E.T. Is Holly our extraterrestrial? Maybe. Or maybe she's just an awesome woman from this planet.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just had a positive first impression of Holly despite his HR prejudice
jokes.punchline: His theological rethink about HR leads to the E.T. comparison — Michael processes changed opinion through movie metaphors, ending with the endearingly earnest 'just an awesome woman from this planet'
jokes.explanation: Michael's thought process here is quintessentially Michael — big pop culture frame, tortured metaphor, genuine sweetness underneath. The E.T. analogy is unexpected and charming. The deflation at the end ('just an awesome woman from this planet') is a great button.

jokes.text: Michael tells Holly that Kevin is 'here on a special work program. He's slow, you know, in his brain.' Holly responds: 'Oh, good for you guys.'
jokes.setup: Michael is hazing Holly by convincing her Kevin has an intellectual disability
jokes.punchline: Holly responds with genuine, patronizing praise: 'Oh, good for you guys' — she's completely taken in, and her well-meaning condescension is the cringe payoff
jokes.explanation: This begins one of the episode's best running gags — Holly believing Kevin has a developmental disability. Her 'good for you guys' is pitch-perfect cringe, and the joke cleverly makes Holly both sympathetic (well-meaning) and complicit in Michael's cruelty. The discomfort is earned.

jokes.text: Kevin offers Holly M&Ms: 'I keep them here at my desk so that everybody doesn't take them.' Holly: 'Well, that is a very safe place for them.'
jokes.setup: Holly now believes Kevin has an intellectual disability; Kevin offers her M&Ms matter-of-factly
jokes.punchline: Holly responds to Kevin's perfectly normal statement ('I keep them here so people don't take them') as if it's a remarkable achievement — 'That is a very safe place for them' delivered with exaggerated encouragement
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the Kevin disability prank. Holly's patronizing response to completely mundane Kevin logic is the cringe engine of this running gag. Works because Kevin is being Kevin — the joke is entirely on Holly's misreading.

jokes.text: Michael: 'You know, if we hung Holly from the ceiling, we'd have to kiss underneath of her.'
jokes.setup: Michael sees Holly and is smitten; says her name out loud
jokes.punchline: Michael makes a mistletoe/holly pun: hanging 'Holly' from the ceiling and kissing under her
jokes.explanation: A classic Michael Scott pun — simultaneously charming and creepy. The pun itself is mild but Michael's complete lack of self-awareness about how it sounds is the real joke.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Are you real, or are you a Hollygram?'
jokes.setup: Michael is flirting with Holly immediately after the mistletoe pun
jokes.punchline: 'Hollygram' — a portmanteau of Holly's name and hologram
jokes.explanation: 'Hollygram' is one of the best Michael Scott wordplay moments — perfectly economical, genuinely clever for Michael, and Holly's response ('I've never heard that one before, actually') is a perfect button. The pun is bad in a good way. High quotability.

jokes.text: Michael to Holly: 'What is your commute like? How long does it take to get in? You know, I should make you a mix. Do you have a CD player?'
jokes.setup: Michael is falling hard for Holly and spiraling into rapid-fire, endearingly awkward questions
jokes.punchline: The pivot from 'commute' to 'I should make you a mix' is a perfect non-sequitur that reveals Michael's chaotic romantic processing
jokes.explanation: Good Michael romantic-confusion comedy. The pivot to 'I should make you a mix' is charming and character-specific — Michael as a 1990s romantic.

jokes.text: Toby shows Michael a group photo: 'It's a photo of everyone in the office so you can take it to Costa Rica.' Michael is not in the photo. Toby: 'Well, I was taking the picture.'
jokes.setup: Toby gives Michael a going-away gift — a group photo of the office
jokes.punchline: Michael isn't in the photo because Toby took it — which either means Toby deliberately excluded Michael or is oblivious; either reading is darkly funny
jokes.explanation: Nicely ambiguous joke — the audience can read Toby's 'well, I was taking the picture' as pathetic (genuinely didn't think of it) or passive-aggressive. Both readings are funny. Good use of the Michael-Toby dynamic.

jokes.text: Jim to David Wallace: 'Congratulations.' Wallace: 'Don't interrupt. Congratulations on doing your job.'
jokes.setup: Jim offers an enthusiastic 'congratulations' on a big sale
jokes.punchline: Wallace dismisses the congratulations as unnecessary — 'doing your job' isn't praiseworthy — undercutting Jim's attempt at warmth
jokes.explanation: Brief but sharp. 'Congratulations on doing your job' is a nicely corporate put-down. Context adds to it (Wallace is otherwise a nice character, making his curtness funnier).

jokes.text: Michael on making a CD mix for Holly, explaining it works 'on two levels': 'Welcome to Scranton' and 'I love you.'
jokes.setup: Michael says he's making Holly a mix CD that 'works on two levels'
jokes.punchline: The two levels are 'welcome to Scranton' and 'I love you' — a wildly disproportionate romantic declaration for someone he just met
jokes.explanation: The gap between 'welcome to Scranton' and 'I love you' as co-equal levels is the joke, and it's a great one. Michael's romantic intensity at zero-acquaintance is perfectly Michael. The buildup and reveal structure works.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Was that U2?' Jim: 'Yes.' Michael: '...You don't love Holly.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks what rock band from Scranton made it big; Jim sarcastically says U2
jokes.punchline: Michael accepts U2 as being from Scranton, then immediately pivots to 'you don't love Holly' — as if these two non-sequiturs are connected
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny — Michael's casual acceptance of a wrong fact, followed by the non-sequitur pivot, is good absurdist comedy but not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: Michael: 'It was love at first see with my ears.'
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining how he fell for Holly — 'it was love at first sight' — then corrects himself because it was her voice
jokes.punchline: 'Love at first see with my ears' — a mangled mixed metaphor that makes its own accidental poetry
jokes.explanation: 'Love at first see with my ears' is a standout Michael Scott line. It's simultaneously broken and poetic — trying to say 'love at first sound' and ending up somewhere beautifully wrong. The self-correction process ('It was love at first sight. Actually no. It was when I heard her voice. It was love at first see with my ears') is structurally excellent. One of the most quotable lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Jim tells Michael to court Holly, then gets lost describing his own history with Pam: 'First time we joked around was at my desk. And the first meal we ever had was...in the break room, actually. We were at two separate tables and I remember that.'
jokes.setup: Jim is giving Michael romantic advice about taking it slow with Holly
jokes.punchline: Jim gets so nostalgic about his own romance with Pam that he trails off, remembering specific tiny details — revealing that the advice is really self-reflection on how much he treasures those ordinary early moments
jokes.explanation: Warm character moment with comedic underpinning — Jim's romantic digression is funny but also touching. The joke is that he's ostensibly coaching Michael but clearly just thinking about Pam. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Andy reveals he's going to propose to Angela tonight; Phyllis's reaction is 'Holy crap!'
jokes.setup: Andy explains he's paying for fireworks at the party — 'I'm going to propose tonight'
jokes.punchline: Phyllis's 'Holy crap!' reaction — a rare outburst that registers the absurdity of the Angela/Andy situation for the audience
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the audience awareness — we know Angela and Dwight are secretly still together. Phyllis's 'Holy crap' serves as the proxy audience reaction. Good structural joke even if the humor depends heavily on series context.

jokes.text: Holly helps Kevin at the vending machine — he has 75 cents, she explains what he can get from the 'top row', and speaks to him with extreme patience
jokes.setup: Kevin is at the vending machine, unable to decide; Holly offers to help
jokes.punchline: Holly's exaggerated patience ('Okay, let's see. 50... This is a button... 55, 65... You have 75 cents. So that means you could get anything on the top row') plays as cringe comedy — she's being condescending to a fully functional adult
jokes.explanation: This is the best execution of the Kevin/Holly running gag. Holly's patient money-counting with Kevin is precisely constructed cringe — she's genuinely trying to help, Kevin is genuinely helpless (but not for the reason she thinks), and the comedy of errors is escalating properly. High rewatch value.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'I am totally gonna bang Holly! She is cute and helpful and she really seems into me.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just been through several charming interactions with Holly
jokes.punchline: Michael summarizes his romantic feelings in the most graceless possible terms — 'bang' vs. all the genuine sweetness of his actual feelings shown in the episode
jokes.explanation: Funny for the gap between Michael's genuine warmth and his crass self-expression. The joke is the tonal whiplash — we just saw all this sweetness and his private summary is 'I am totally gonna bang Holly.' Character-consistent.

jokes.text: Jim leaves a message for Ryan: 'I don't know what you got lately, but I really don't care because you're trying to get rid of me... I bet you think I don't care enough about this job to actually fight back, but you're wrong.'
jokes.setup: Jim has discovered Ryan has been trying to push him out and leaves a defiant voicemail
jokes.punchline: The voicemail is blustery and tough — immediately followed by Jim realizing Ryan has been arrested (and thus the message is irrelevant and now recorded evidence), shown by his 'Damn it!'
jokes.explanation: The dramatic voicemail deflated by immediate circumstances is a well-worn structure but executed well here. The 'Damn it!' revelation works because of the timing.

jokes.text: Jim's second voicemail to Ryan: 'Totally disregard that last voice mail because you obviously have your hands tied.'
jokes.setup: Jim just left a tough voicemail for Ryan, then learned Ryan was arrested
jokes.punchline: 'Your hands are obviously tied' — a dry acknowledgment that Ryan is literally in police custody, retconning his dramatic message as a misunderstanding
jokes.explanation: 'Your hands are obviously tied' is a great line — the understatement is perfect (Ryan is under arrest), and Jim's pivot from tough guy to damage-control is pure Jim. The economy is excellent — a lot of comedy packed into very few words. Good wry callback.

jokes.text: Holly explaining why she's on the floor: 'I tried to adjust the lumbar support on Toby's chair, and that made this up/down lever thing not work. And then I took the whole chair apart, and...that is the story of me on the floor. It's pretty good, right? I'm gonna sell the movie rights.'
jokes.setup: Michael finds Holly sitting on the floor surrounded by a disassembled chair
jokes.punchline: 'That is the story of me on the floor. It's pretty good, right? I'm gonna sell the movie rights' — Holly sells an embarrassing situation as a charming origin story
jokes.explanation: 'I'm gonna sell the movie rights' is a very funny self-deprecating line — Holly is quick-witted and funny in exactly the way Michael wishes he was. This establishes the romantic compatibility efficiently and comedically.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly do Yoda impressions while assembling the chair: 'Sit on floor and put together chair we will.' / 'Yo-da.' / 'Pass curvy metal piece you will.'
jokes.setup: Holly is on the floor with a disassembled chair; Michael joins her
jokes.punchline: They spontaneously fall into doing Yoda impressions together while building the chair — establishing an immediate comedic wavelength between them
jokes.explanation: Charming scene — the Yoda bits aren't hilarious individually but the moment as a whole is comedically effective in establishing Michael and Holly's chemistry. 'Yo-da' as a button after the first Yoda-speak line is particularly nice.

jokes.text: Michael: 'So you can't make my orgy?' pause 'Kidding.' pause 'Acting!' Holly: 'Acting!' Both: 'Lovitz.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Holly if she's in town this weekend; nervous, he blurts out 'So you can't make my orgy?'
jokes.punchline: Michael's desperate recovery — 'Kidding. Acting! Acting!' — and Holly joining in the 'Lovitz' reference shows they're on the exact same comedic page
jokes.explanation: Delightful moment — Michael's social panic recovers into something that accidentally works perfectly. Holly immediately completing his Jon Lovitz reference ('Lovitz') is a precision-crafted romantic beat disguised as a comedy moment. High impact for a room that's invested in this pairing.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head about his exit interview prep: 'Toby has been cruisin' for a bruisin' for 12 years, and I am now his cruise director. And my name is Captain Bruisin'.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been looking forward to Toby's exit interview for years
jokes.punchline: 'I am now his cruise director. And my name is Captain Bruisin'' — Michael extends the cruisin'/bruisin' rhyme into a nautical metaphor, proud of his own wordplay
jokes.explanation: Michael's self-satisfaction with terrible wordplay is very on-brand. 'Captain Bruisin'' is gloriously stupid and the nautical extension of 'cruisin'' is exactly Michael's type of pun inflation.

jokes.text: Michael's exit interview opening: 'Of all the idiots in all the idiot villages in all the idiot worlds, you stand alone, my friend.'
jokes.setup: Michael begins Toby's formal exit interview
jokes.punchline: Instead of a standard opening question, Michael delivers a theatrical monologue escalating Casablanca's structure to call Toby the ultimate idiot across all universes
jokes.explanation: One of the best Michael-insults-Toby constructions in the series. The Casablanca riff ('of all the gin joints') applied to Toby is perfectly structured — the escalation from 'idiot villages' to 'idiot worlds' is absurdly funny. Michael's theatrical preparation for this moment pays off with a genuinely quotable insult. Strong craft.

jokes.text: Michael's first exit interview question: a long dramatic pause, then: 'Who do you think you are?'
jokes.setup: Michael has the standard HR exit interview binder; opens it dramatically
jokes.punchline: After maximum build-up and a long pause (implied from the timestamp gap [21:01]), his first 'question' is the existential non-question: 'Who do you think you are?'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The dramatic pause (implied by context), followed by the non-question 'Who do you think you are?' — deeply philosophical yet deeply petty — is perfectly Michael. Toby's deadpan 'I'm Toby' / Michael's 'Correct' exchange is exceptional. The structure of long wind-up → absurd question → literal answer → deflation is masterful. High rewatch value.

jokes.text: Toby: 'I'm Toby.' Michael: 'Yeah. Correct.'
jokes.setup: Michael asked 'Who do you think you are?' — Toby answers literally
jokes.punchline: Michael confirms the answer with 'Yeah. Correct.' — as if this was a valid interview answer and he's moving on
jokes.explanation: The deadpan perfection of 'Yeah. Correct.' after Toby's literal self-identification is one of the best two-word punchlines in the episode. Economy is a 10 — maximum comedy per word. The rhythm of Michael's build-up, the absurd question, Toby's literal answer, and Michael's bureaucratic confirmation is impeccably timed.

jokes.text: Michael's next question: extended pause then 'What gives...what...what gives you the right?'
jokes.setup: Michael is working through his 'questions' in the exit interview
jokes.punchline: His second prepared question is another existential non-question: 'What gives you the right?' — equally unanswerable and petty
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the exit interview absurdity. 'What gives you the right?' is another existential non-question, continuing Michael's pattern. Slightly diminishing returns from joke 46 but still very funny. The trailing pauses before delivery add to the comedy.

jokes.text: Michael's follow-up question: 'What gives... What... What gives you the right?'
jokes.setup: Having established that Toby is in fact Toby, Michael moves to his next prepared grievance
jokes.punchline: His second question is 'What gives you the right?' — equally non-specific, equally accusatory, equally meaningless as an HR question
jokes.explanation: Good follow-up to the 'who do you think you are' exchange. The pattern is established and the second vacuous grievance lands because we now know Michael's entire prepared interview is existential accusations. The stuttering delivery ('What gives... What... What gives you the right?') suggests Michael is reading from a mental list.

jokes.text: Michael reads aloud: 'What would you improve about Dunder Mifflin?' then says: 'I'll kill you.'
jokes.setup: Holly introduces the standard exit interview binder; Michael reads from it aloud
jokes.punchline: Upon reading 'What would you improve about Dunder Mifflin?' and seeing Toby start to answer, Michael skips the standard HR script and says 'I'll kill you' — apparently to prevent any criticism of the office
jokes.explanation: 'I'll kill you' is an exceptional button to the exit interview sequence. The absurdity of reading a standard HR question aloud and responding to Toby's attempt to answer with a death threat — plus the delivery timing — makes this a standout. Three words, enormous impact. High quotability.

jokes.text: Michael gives Toby a box labeled 'Suck on this.' Michael: 'That is not even my handwriting.'
jokes.setup: Michael tells Toby to open his present; it's a wrapped rock with a note reading 'Suck on this'
jokes.punchline: When everyone's horrified, Michael denies writing the note: 'That's not even my handwriting' — as if the handwriting is the problem and not the sentiment
jokes.explanation: Good Michael moment — the rock-as-gift with 'Suck on this' is broadly dark, and Michael's disavowal focusing on handwriting rather than content is classic misdirection of his own culpability.

jokes.text: Michael: 'You know what that is? You know what that is? That is...a psyche. Psyche.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is horrified that Michael gave Toby a rock labeled 'Suck on this'; Michael panics
jokes.punchline: Michael retroactively declares it a 'psyche' — a 1990s fake-out — but does so so lamely and obviously that it makes it worse
jokes.explanation: Michael's panicked 'psyche' recovery is funny mainly for the desperation behind it. Classic Michael trying to retroactively avoid consequences. Functional.

jokes.text: Michael gives away his watch as his 'real gift' to Toby; Pam guesses 'Your watch?' before he says it. Michael: 'How did you know?' Pam: 'I just knew.'
jokes.setup: Michael scrambles to produce a 'real' gift after the rock embarrassment; announces he'll give Toby 'something special'
jokes.punchline: Pam guesses 'Your watch?' before he even says it — indicating his gift is so predictably impulsive that it's obvious. Michael's genuine bewilderment at being known this well is sweet and funny.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Pam knowing Michael well enough to predict his impulsive gift, and Michael's genuine surprise at being read, is sweet and funny. Shows Pam's quiet wisdom about her office family.

jokes.text: Ryan is being led away by police; Kelly: 'Oh my god. I cannot wait to visit Ryan in prison. I'm gonna wear my hottest track suit and get my hair done. And then be like, Hi Ryan. And then all the other prisoners are gonna be like, Damn! Ryan, you got a hot ex-girlfriend. I would never have treated her so bad when I was outside of prison.'
jokes.setup: Ryan Howard is being arrested for fraud in the parking lot
jokes.punchline: Kelly immediately fantasizes in elaborate detail about her prison visit as a social triumph, complete with the other prisoners' imagined dialogue
jokes.explanation: Classic Kelly speech — entirely self-centered, completely elaborated, and somehow both vindictive and earnest. The detail of 'my hottest track suit' and ventriloquizing the other prisoners ('Damn! Ryan, you got a hot ex-girlfriend') is pitch-perfect Kelly Kapoor. High impact in a room — this is a fan-favorite Kelly moment.

jokes.text: Dwight on Ryan's fraud arrest: 'The real crime, I think, was the beard.'
jokes.setup: People are discussing Ryan being arrested for misleading shareholders/fraud
jokes.punchline: Dwight cuts through all the serious legal analysis to identify the true crime: Ryan's facial hair
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The economy is exceptional — five words that redirect a major plot moment into absurdity. Dwight's priorities being aesthetics over fraud is perfectly character-integrated. Very high quotability. This line would get a genuine laugh from almost any room.

jokes.text: Holly comforts Michael about Ryan; Michael: 'I'm holding it together. I have a business to run. I'm cool.' Holly: 'No, hey, stop. You can let yourself be upset. He's your friend.'
jokes.setup: Holly notices Michael is upset about Ryan being arrested
jokes.punchline: Holly's genuine, simple kindness — 'you can let yourself be upset' — cuts through Michael's bluster and nearly makes him cry. The comedy is Michael's emotional transparency and how easily Holly reaches him.
jokes.explanation: More tender than funny, but the comedy is in Michael's complete inability to maintain his 'I'm cool' facade. Works as character comedy even if the laugh is gentle.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Holly is sweet and simple. Like a lady baker. I would not be surprised to find out that she had worked in a bakery before coming here. She has that kind of warmth. I'm pretty sure she's baked on a professional level.'
jokes.setup: Michael is reflecting on Holly's warmth and kindness
jokes.punchline: Michael's attempt to articulate Holly's warmth becomes an increasingly committed theory that she is a professional baker — 'I'm pretty sure she's baked on a professional level' delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Michael's thought spiral from 'she's warm' to 'she has definitely baked professionally' is good absurdist character work. The escalating confidence ('I'm pretty sure she's baked on a professional level') is very Michael. The 'lady baker' coinage is specific and funny.

jokes.text: Kevin runs toward and presumably jumps into the bouncy house at the party
jokes.setup: Phyllis has arranged a bouncy house at the parking lot party
jokes.punchline: Kevin's enthusiastic 'Cool! A bouncy house!' followed by presumably leaping in immediately (before being told to take his shoes off) is a visual gag about Kevin's childlike impulsiveness
jokes.explanation: 'Kevin, take your shoes off first' implies Kevin has already launched himself in — his enthusiasm and lack of social filtering is consistently good Kevin character comedy.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam: 'Is Jim gonna propose tonight? He is, isn't he? No, he's not. Is he?'
jokes.setup: Andy has just revealed he's going to propose at the party; Pam and Jim react
jokes.punchline: The rapid back-and-forth between Pam and Jim (or Pam to camera) — the quick 'no he's not / is he?' — plays as a comedic beat that both teases the audience and reveals Pam's hope
jokes.explanation: Functional comedy with high emotional stakes — works because the audience has been waiting for the Jim proposal all season, so 'Is he? / No he's not / Is he?' is both funny and emotionally charged.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam exchange: 'It was easy to get in, but impossible to rise up. That's what she...' 'A lot of places are like that.'
jokes.setup: Jim is talking about his old company; sets up the 'that's what she said' punchline
jokes.punchline: He catches himself ('That's what she...') but Pam smoothly deflects with 'A lot of places are like that' — Jim's interrupted self-censorship on Michael's catchphrase is the joke
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed 'that's what she said' subversion — Jim almost says it (a Michael catchphrase) then stops, and Pam covers with a straight line. Works on two levels: the almost-joke and the implication that Jim has been corrupted by Michael. Good economy.

jokes.text: Dwight has put a raccoon in Holly's car as 'playful hazing.' Holly runs away screaming; Michael: 'There is a raccoon in the car, Dwight!' Dwight: 'No, there's not.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has executed a hazing prank on Holly involving what is clearly a raccoon in her car
jokes.punchline: Dwight's straight-faced 'No, there's not' denial of the obviously present raccoon is classically absurd. 'There is no such thing as playful hazing' from Michael — who was in on it — is hypocritical and funny.
jokes.explanation: Solid physical comedy beat — Dwight's flat denial of what everyone can see is good Dwight. Michael's 'no such thing as playful hazing' hypocrisy adds to it.

jokes.text: Michael's speech about Holly: 'Holly is the best thing that has happened to this company since World War II.'
jokes.setup: Michael is publicly defending Holly after the raccoon incident
jokes.punchline: His hyperbolic compliment frames Holly's arrival as historically significant — 'since World War II' — an absurd benchmark for a new HR hire
jokes.explanation: Good Michael hyperbole — comparing an HR rep's arrival to WWII ending is beautifully disproportionate. Works as character comedy and establishes how smitten Michael is.

jokes.text: During Michael's heartfelt speech to Holly, Dwight in background: 'It's not rabid.'
jokes.setup: Michael is delivering a touching speech about how much Holly means to him/the company; Dwight is presumably still dealing with the raccoon situation
jokes.punchline: 'It's not rabid' — Dwight's matter-of-fact interjection into an emotional moment, prioritizing raccoon health data
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous comedic impact. The juxtaposition of Michael's sincere emotional declaration with Dwight's background raccoon update ('It's not rabid') is perfectly timed deadpan. Classic comedy of context — the mundane intrusion on the dramatic is a beloved comedic device, and this is one of the episode's best executions. High quotability.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Well, Jan didn't believe in showing affection, so sometimes I don't know how to react when a girl touches me. I like it.'
jokes.setup: Holly briefly touched Michael's arm in a comforting way; Michael reacted visibly
jokes.punchline: 'I like it' — delivered after explaining his affection deprivation, the simple declaration is unexpectedly touching and funny
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most effective Michael lines — the economy of 'I like it' after the Jan context is perfect. It's simultaneously sad, funny, and endearing. High character integration — only Michael would need to clarify that he enjoys being touched positively.

jokes.text: Kevin drives his own car to the store. Holly is surprised. Kevin confirms: 'Yup, this is my car.' Holly: 'Do you drive your own car?' Kevin: 'Yep, just like you.' Holly: 'Okay, bye.' Kevin: 'Bye.'
jokes.setup: Holly still believes Kevin has an intellectual disability; he's driving himself to the store
jokes.punchline: Holly's shocked 'do you drive your own car?' and Kevin's cheerful 'just like you' — followed by the world's most awkward goodbye — is peak running-gag cringe
jokes.explanation: Strong running gag payoff — 'Just like you' from Kevin is an accidental masterpiece of unintentional condescension reversal. Kevin, completely oblivious to what Holly thinks, is just describing reality; Holly's reading of it as an achievement is the cringe engine. The final 'bye / bye' is a beautifully awkward button.

jokes.text: Darryl's talking head: 'I'm really proud of you.' — after watching Kevin drive away
jokes.setup: Kevin has successfully driven himself to the store
jokes.punchline: Darryl, watching Kevin drive, delivers 'I'm really proud of you' — possibly genuinely (Kevin sometimes needs support) or joining in Holly's misreading without knowing it
jokes.explanation: Excellent deadpan button on the Kevin sequence. Five words with perfect timing. Darryl's sincere-seeming pride in Kevin's basic life skill extends the cringe/disability confusion joke perfectly.

jokes.text: Michael's song parody credits: 'I have done things like... Beers in heaven. Classic. Or Total eclipse of the fart. Not my favorite, but...'
jokes.setup: Michael introduces himself as an 'accomplished song parody writer' before performing a song for Toby
jokes.punchline: His examples: 'Beers in Heaven' and 'Total Eclipse of the Fart' — one genuinely clever, one juvenile but specific
jokes.explanation: The distinction between 'Beers in Heaven' (which is actually clever wordplay) and 'Total Eclipse of the Fart' (which Michael himself damns with faint praise: 'Not my favorite, but...') is perfectly Michael Scott. His self-assessment of his own work as a mixed catalog is great character writing.

jokes.text: Michael's party speech: 'Now, a lot of you know that I am an accomplished songwriter. Song parody writer. I have done things like Beers in Heaven. Classic. Or Total Eclipse of the Fart.'
jokes.setup: Michael is introducing a special tribute song for Toby at the party
jokes.punchline: 'Total Eclipse of the Fart' — Michael's song parody titles are juvenile malapropisms; 'Beers in Heaven' and 'Total Eclipse of the Fart' are obvious bad puns delivered with enormous pride
jokes.explanation: 'Total Eclipse of the Fart' is a very Michael title — proud of a terrible fart joke, calling it classic. The self-assessment 'not my favorite, but' adds to it. Good character comedy, very quotable.

jokes.text: Michael performs 'Goodbye, Toby' to the tune of 'Goodbye Stranger' by Supertramp; coworkers give confessionals during the song
jokes.setup: Michael performs his original Toby tribute song at the party
jokes.punchline: While Michael sings sincerely, intercut confessionals reveal: Kelly 'I'm gonna miss Toby. He has a nice, calming presence' and Angela 'Don't tell him I said this, but I always thought he was kinda cute' — both undercut the idea that Toby is universally despised
jokes.explanation: The structural comedy of Michael's sincere (if bizarre) tribute intercut with people actually liking Toby is well-executed. Angela's 'I always thought he was kinda cute' in particular is a great character surprise.

jokes.text: Michael to Holly: 'Someday I would love to hear Beers in Heaven.' Holly: 'Oh, okay. Yeah.' Michael: 'Well, actually, too soon. It's...very sexual.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are chatting post-performance; she asks about Beers in Heaven
jokes.punchline: 'Too soon. It's very sexual.' — the implication that Michael's parody of 'Tears in Heaven' is both too soon (Eric Clapton's son died) AND sexual is a great layered absurdity
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback joke. The reveal that 'Beers in Heaven' is both 'too soon' (nodding to its source material) AND 'very sexual' is perfectly absurd. The 'too soon' shows Michael has some cultural awareness; 'it's very sexual' subverts any credit. One of the funnier Michael one-two punchlines in the episode.

jokes.text: Kevin calls Michael to the supermarket: there's Jan, very pregnant. Kevin: 'I think you kids have a lot to catch up on.'
jokes.setup: Kevin called Michael away from the party saying something 'needs to be seen'; Michael arrives at the supermarket to find Jan, very pregnant
jokes.punchline: Kevin's matchmaking delivery — 'I think you kids have a lot to catch up on' — is completely out of character for Kevin; he's playing wise advisor for one moment
jokes.explanation: Good comedic pivot — Kevin's scheming and the delivery of 'you kids have a lot to catch up on' is funny because of how un-Kevin it is. The situation itself (pregnant Jan at the supermarket) is the bigger comedic payoff.

jokes.text: Michael upon seeing Jan pregnant: 'Are you nauseous? Do you have cravings? You never touched my Propecia or my Accutane?'
jokes.setup: Michael sees Jan is very pregnant; starts rapid-firing questions
jokes.punchline: 'You never touched my Propecia or my Accutane?' — Michael's first worry about the pregnancy is whether his hair-loss medication or acne treatment could be the cause
jokes.explanation: Michael's concern about Propecia/Accutane is very specific and funny — he's not asking about the baby's father, he's worried about his toiletries. The specificity of the brand names makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Well, okay. So it's not mine, and it's not somebody else's, so...I know the whole toilet seat thing is a myth, so... I went to a sperm bank.'
jokes.setup: Jan tells Michael he's not the father; Michael tries to work out the logic
jokes.punchline: Michael's reasoning process: (1) not mine, (2) not someone else's, (3) therefore toilet seat? Before Jan corrects with sperm bank. Michael's genuine consideration of the toilet seat myth as an explanation is beautifully stupid.
jokes.explanation: Michael's logical chain — ruling out other fathers, briefly landing on 'toilet seat myth' as a genuine possibility — is wonderfully stupid. The self-correction 'I know the whole toilet seat thing is a myth' shows he has partial information but applies it wrong. Strong absurdist character logic.

jokes.text: Jan explains she went to a sperm bank while they were dating. Michael: 'I know the whole toilet seat thing is a myth, so...'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to process how Jan got pregnant not by him and not by cheating
jokes.punchline: Michael lands on 'I know the whole toilet seat thing is a myth' — meaning he's actually considering that Jan could have gotten pregnant from a toilet seat before arriving at sperm bank
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's absolute best moments. Michael, faced with 'not cheating and not me,' processes through: toilet seat (dismisses it as a myth) → sperm bank. The fact that the toilet seat was a serious hypothesis he had to rule out reveals the full extent of Michael's sexual ignorance. 'I know the whole toilet seat thing is a myth, so...' delivered as a thoughtful process of elimination is Michael Scott at his finest. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Michael: 'When we were going out, you'd rather have somebody else's sperm than mine?' Jan: 'No, no. It's not just any sperm bank...it's right next to that little breakfast place in the city where you can draw on the tables.' Michael: 'IHOP.'
jokes.setup: Michael is hurt that Jan used a sperm bank instead of him; Jan tries to soften it by describing the location
jokes.punchline: Jan's description 'that little breakfast place in the city where you can draw on the tables' is answered by Michael with 'IHOP' — which (a) is wrong (IHOP doesn't have draw-on-tables) and (b) the specificity of his confident wrong answer is funny
jokes.explanation: Michael confidently answering 'IHOP' to a description that doesn't match IHOP is a great Michael beat — wrong but certain. The digression about breakfast places in the middle of an emotionally devastating revelation is tonally perfect absurdism.

jokes.text: Michael can't understand why Jan used a sperm bank instead of him: 'You'd rather have somebody else's sperm than mine?' Jan: 'No, no, no. It's not just any sperm bank. It's a really, really great place. It's amazing, actually. I'm gonna bring you the catalogue.'
jokes.setup: Michael is hurt that Jan chose a sperm bank over him
jokes.punchline: Jan's attempt to reassure Michael that it's a QUALITY sperm bank — 'I'll bring you the catalogue' — treats the situation as a product recommendation
jokes.explanation: Jan's pivot to sperm bank quality assurance ('I'll bring you the catalogue') is both tone-deaf and perfectly Jan. Her matter-of-factness about an objectively bizarre social situation is her defining character trait deployed perfectly here.

jokes.text: Jan: 'It's right next to that little breakfast place that you like in the city where you can draw on the tables.' Michael: 'Ihop.'
jokes.setup: Jan is trying to describe the sperm bank's location using landmarks Michael would recognize
jokes.punchline: She describes IHOP as 'that little breakfast place... where you can draw on the tables' — a weirdly precious description of IHOP — and Michael simply replies 'IHOP'
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great comedic beat. Jan's refined way of describing IHOP ('that little breakfast place where you can draw on the tables') is perfect character comedy for her pretentious persona. Michael's flat 'Ihop' is the ideal punchline — deadpan, one word, complete. The joke also implies Michael considers IHOP a significant landmark, which is its own character detail. Exceptional economy.

jokes.text: Jan: 'If I was 22 and had lots of time to have lots of children, then sure, let's let Michael have a shot at one. But honestly, I need to make this one count.'
jokes.setup: Jan is explaining why she went to a sperm bank instead of using Michael
jokes.punchline: 'Let's let Michael have a shot at one. But I need to make this one count' — brutally dismissive of Michael's genetic viability, framed as a purely practical decision
jokes.explanation: 'I need to make this one count' as Jan's reason for not using Michael is devastatingly funny — simultaneously cruel and perfectly Jan. High quotability.

jokes.text: Jan: 'I usually, you know, use a foam noodle instead of a partner' in lamaze class
jokes.setup: Jan invites Michael to her lamaze class
jokes.punchline: Jan's casual admission that she uses a pool noodle as her lamaze partner — rather than a human — reveals her social isolation after Michael
jokes.explanation: Good darkly comic detail about Jan's post-Michael life. The foam noodle detail is specific and sad in a funny way.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'My whole life, I have known two things. I love sex. And I want to have kids. And I always thought those two things would go hand in hand. But now I think it might be one or the other.'
jokes.setup: Michael processes Jan's pregnancy and the sperm bank revelation
jokes.punchline: The existential crisis about whether he can have sex AND children — framed as two competing life values — is deeply, inadvertently dark
jokes.explanation: 'I always thought those two things would go hand in hand' — the premise is funny because it SHOULD go together (sex leads to children) but Michael has managed to separate them completely. His genuine existential crisis about it is darkly comic.

jokes.text: Phyllis to Michael after the party: 'Well, I hope you had fun today. 'Cause you're never ever throwing a party again.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis has just executed the whole party despite Michael's interference
jokes.punchline: Phyllis delivers her verdict with quiet finality — 'never ever throwing a party again' — as Michael visibly deflated
jokes.explanation: Good Phyllis moment — her quiet authority in party planning matters, and the finality of her verdict, is well-executed. Brief but satisfying.

jokes.text: Andy proposes to Angela with his parents present ('Andrew and Ellen Bernard, thank you for sharing this joyous moment'), full PA announcement, then asks her to 'join me onstage'; she doesn't move; he says 'Okay then I will come to you, my flower.' She says 'okay' into the mic barely audibly.
jokes.setup: Andy proposes to Angela in front of the entire office with fireworks, a band, his parents present, and a PA system
jokes.punchline: Angela's unenthusiastic 'okay' — barely audible, utterly joyless — after the most elaborate proposal setup imaginable is devastating cringe comedy
jokes.explanation: One of the great cringe moments of the series. The elaborate setup (parents, band, fireworks, PA) vs. Angela's monosyllabic reluctant 'okay' is peak Office comedy. The audience knows Angela is secretly still with Dwight, which makes her joyless acceptance absolutely devastating. Andy's 'Into the mike, sweetie' / 'I said okay' / 'She said yes!' cascade is perfectly structured. High impact.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Damn it!' — trips or stumbles going toward Angela to propose
jokes.setup: Andy dramatically announces he'll come to Angela on the dance floor
jokes.punchline: He immediately stumbles or trips — inferred from 'Damn it!' — undercutting his romantic moment
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe comedy — Andy's grand romantic moment immediately undercut by physical comedy. 'Damn it!' in the middle of a proposal is very Andy Bernard. Functional slapstick that lands because of the character stakes.

jokes.text: Andy's proposal: 'Angela, will you do me the honor of giving me your tiny hand in marriage?'
jokes.setup: Andy proposes to Angela at the party
jokes.punchline: 'Your tiny hand' — Andy specifically and unnecessarily notes the smallness of Angela's hand in the marriage proposal
jokes.explanation: The detail 'your tiny hand' in a marriage proposal is unexpectedly funny. It's a genuine physical description of Angela (she is small) that Andy has apparently written into his prepared proposal speech. The specificity of 'tiny' as a proposal flourish is absurd and quotable. Very good character integration for Andy's earnest idiosyncratic romanticism.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'I've been carrying that ring around in my wallet for six years. Because you don't know when you're gonna meet the right girl and the moment's gonna be right.'
jokes.setup: Andy explains the ring he used for the proposal
jokes.punchline: He's been carrying an engagement ring in his wallet for six years — a detail that's simultaneously romantic and alarming, implying he's been ready to propose to anyone for years
jokes.explanation: Six years of carrying the ring implies the proposal was less about Angela specifically and more about Andy's general readiness. Darkly funny character detail.

jokes.text: Kelly runs up to Andy: 'Can I be your bridesmaid?' Andy: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Andy celebrates the engagement; Kelly rushes up enthusiastically
jokes.punchline: Andy's flat 'No' to Kelly's bridesmaid question — instantaneous and absolute — is a perfect deadpan
jokes.explanation: The immediate 'No' without hesitation is a great button. Economy is exceptional. Funny because Andy is usually desperate for approval — his refusal of Kelly shows his obliviousness rather than genuine decisiveness.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'Well... It's my own fault.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just proposed to Angela; Dwight is secretly her ongoing lover and knows this is his fault for not committing
jokes.punchline: Dwight's devastated, resigned 'It's my own fault' — the most loaded three-word confessional in the episode
jokes.explanation: One of the best talking heads in the episode. The comedy comes entirely from context — Dwight's resigned self-blame is funny because the audience knows he's Angela's secret lover and the tragedy is entirely self-inflicted. 'Well... It's my own fault.' with the pause is perfectly delivered. Economy is 9.5 — no words wasted. Among the top moments of the episode.

jokes.text: Andy to Jim: 'Tuna! I'm engaged!' Jim: 'I know. That's awesome, man. That's great.' Andy: 'Mr. Andrew Bernard. It's got a nice ring to it.'
jokes.setup: Andy celebrates his engagement with Jim
jokes.punchline: 'It's got a nice ring to it' — Andy's accidental engagement pun on 'ring'
jokes.explanation: The pun 'got a nice ring to it' after a proposal is not very original, but Andy's apparent unawareness of his own pun and his genuine self-admiration saves it slightly.

jokes.text: Meredith takes photo: 'Oh let's do it again. Pam, your smile is weird.' Pam: 'It's digital, so just take as many as you want.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are having a photo taken together; Pam holds the camera
jokes.punchline: Meredith's blunt 'Pam, your smile is weird' — said to someone not in the photo — followed by Pam's patient 'it's digital' redirect is a good background character beat
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny Meredith cameo — her bluntness is character-consistent. The 'your smile is weird' directed at someone not being photographed is a good small gag.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'I don't know, I just...I really thought Jim was gonna propose tonight.'
jokes.setup: The party is winding down; Andy got engaged to Angela
jokes.punchline: Pam's quiet disappointment that Jim didn't propose — she was hoping tonight would be the night
jokes.explanation: Bittersweet comedic beat — Pam's visible disappointment is played for both laughs and emotion. Works because of series context, and because we know (from the episode) that Jim has something planned.

jokes.text: Holly's end-of-day talking head: 'Well, I can see Andy proposing to Angela. I can also see him proposing to Oscar. So...'
jokes.setup: Holly is reflecting on Andy's proposal on her first day
jokes.punchline: Holly, new to the office, considers Oscar as a plausible Andy proposal target — implying she can't read the office dynamics at all yet
jokes.explanation: Great Holly talking head — she's observant enough to notice something off about the proposal, but new enough that her analysis is wildly off. 'I can also see him proposing to Oscar' is a funny line that both jokes about Oscar and establishes Holly as a fresh perspective.

jokes.text: Michael spontaneously offers to go to the diner with Holly for pie: 'I'll go to the diner with you.' Holly: 'That would be great.' Michael: 'Yeah, we can go eat pie. I love pie.' Holly: 'Me too.'
jokes.setup: Holly mentions going off-campus to get dessert; Michael had been coaching himself not to rush things
jokes.punchline: Michael's earlier resolution to 'lay a base' dissolves completely at the mention of pie — his real-life spontaneity overriding his strategic restraint. 'I love pie' / 'Me too' is a lovely, charming mirror moment.
jokes.explanation: Sweet payoff for the Michael-Holly throughline. The 'I love pie / me too' mirroring is charming and warm. The comedy is in Michael's complete inability to play it cool — his restraint lasts precisely until 'dessert' is mentioned.

jokes.text: Michael asks Holly to get dessert. Holly suggests the Glider Diner. Michael: 'I'll go to the diner with you.' Holly: 'I love pie.' Michael: 'Me too.'
jokes.setup: Holly mentions going somewhere for dessert; she suggests asking Stanley about the Glider Diner
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately volunteers to go — then they discover mutual love of pie, which becomes their first date invitation
jokes.explanation: Sweet and understated. The joke is in how un-smooth Michael's date-getting is — his literal 'I'll go to the diner with you' — and how it still works because Holly is equally direct. The mutual pie declaration is charming. Rewatchable as the beginning of their relationship.

jokes.text: Toby's goodbye to Michael; Michael shows up with a security badge: 'Really, Michael?' Michael: 'Sorry, corporate policy.' Toby: 'It's not.' Michael: 'You might take something.'
jokes.setup: Toby is leaving the building for the last time; Michael appears
jokes.punchline: Michael has come with a security badge to 'escort' Toby out — 'Sorry, corporate policy' / 'It's not' / 'You might take something' is a final petty victory over Toby
jokes.explanation: Good Michael-Toby sendoff joke — Michael's 'you might take something' after 12 years of Toby being a model employee is perfectly petty. The casual dismissal of Toby's 'it's not corporate policy' is well-executed.

jokes.text: Holly's goodbye: 'I gotta buckle him in.' (referring to her dog/pet in the car)
jokes.setup: Holly is saying goodbye at the end of the day
jokes.punchline: 'I gotta buckle him in' — Holly buckles in a pet (dog is implied) like a child, which is endearing and slightly absurd
jokes.explanation: A small, good character detail for Holly — she's the kind of person who buckles her dog in. Fits her warm, slightly eccentric personality. Not a big laugh but a nice character moment.

jokes.text: Michael's voicemail to Jan: 'Hi Jan, it's Michael. I just...I want to let you know that I am going to go to your lamaze class tomorrow. And if there are any details you need to fill me in on, like...what, exactly, lamaze is, that would be great.'
jokes.setup: Michael has decided to support Jan by going to lamaze class
jokes.punchline: He commits to going before knowing what lamaze is — 'what, exactly, lamaze is, that would be great' — Michael's decision-first-research-never approach
jokes.explanation: Good Michael character moment — he commits fully before understanding what he's committed to. 'What exactly lamaze is, that would be great' is a funny admission of complete ignorance paired with full commitment.

jokes.text: Toby's departure triggers some kind of office alarm. Toby and Michael both look confused.
jokes.setup: Toby is finally leaving the building after Michael's security pat-down
jokes.punchline: An alarm goes off as Toby exits — as if the building itself is registering his departure
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy button on the Michael-Toby departure scene. The alarm is probably a coincidence (fire alarm, door alarm) but the timing makes it feel like the building's reaction. Decent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'I am going to be...kind of a daddy.'
jokes.setup: Michael has decided to support Jan through her pregnancy as a lamaze partner
jokes.punchline: 'Kind of a daddy' — the qualifier 'kind of' doing enormous work in this self-assessment; Michael can't fully commit even in his own description of his role
jokes.explanation: One of the best episode-ending lines. 'Kind of a daddy' — the imprecision, the qualifier, the earnest pride beneath the uncertainty — is a perfect Michael Scott sentence. Captures his entire character in four words. Economy is outstanding. Among the most quotable lines of the episode.

jokes.text: Michael's voicemail button: '...I am going to be... kind of a daddy.'
jokes.setup: Michael is processing his decision to be involved with Jan's baby
jokes.punchline: 'Kind of a daddy' — Michael's self-designation as a non-biological quasi-father figure, delivered with tentative sincerity
jokes.explanation: The episode's emotional peak disguised as comedy. 'Kind of a daddy' is three words that contain Michael's entire arc: his longing for family, his uncertainty about his role, his optimism. It's funny because of 'kind of' — the legal/biological hedge — and heartbreaking because of how much he means it. This line is among the most memorable in the episode and possibly in the season. Exceptional character integration and economy.
